en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Dhāraṇī of the One-Braided Honored One.
[Posthumously honored with the title: Grand Master of the Household, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Susuo, with a fief of three thousand households;
invested with purple robes; posthumously appointed as Minister of Works; posthumous title: Dajian (Great Mirror).

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at the Great City of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of the Great Xingshan Temple, who possesses Great and Vast Wisdom, in accordance with imperial decree.
Accompanied by immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
he was surrounded by them from before and behind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara...
Accompanied by countless vidyādhara noble ones,
they surrounded him on all sides and approached the place where the Buddha was; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they stood there.
Prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage at the Buddha’s feet.
Having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
there are various devas, vidyādhara sages,
and others who take the Great Brahmā as their teacher and object of faith."
I wish to subdue the Great Brahmā, the celestial sages, and their like;
may the Buddha grant his permission.
This is because I desire to cause all sentient beings to mindfully contemplate wholesome dharmas.
It is for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to be free from sorrow and affliction;
to eliminate the illnesses of all sentient beings;
and to completely eradicate all obstacles, difficulties, calamities, portents, and evil dreams.
In order to eliminate all untimely deaths and illnesses;
to soften the hearts of all those with evil intentions;
and to ensure that no obstacles or difficulties arise from any demons, ghosts, or deities.
"Blessed One, I now possess a root-heart dhāraṇī that can eliminate the karmic offenses of all sentient beings.
Blessed One, I have never seen anyone— whether a deva, a māra, a Śakra, or a Brahmā— who [could do so]."
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas,
or others who are able to receive and uphold this mantra,
whether by reciting it, copying it, or circulating it.
Or, by means of this dharma, one may protect one's body;
whether entering an army for battle or being harmed by poison.
By upholding this dhāraṇī,
no difficulties whatsoever shall be able to prevail.
Such a teaching is what all Buddhas keep in mind.
"World-Honored One, this dharma of mine, the dhāraṇī,
has already been spoken by immeasurable Buddhas. During my stage as a bodhisattva,
beyond kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
There was a Buddha named Śatapatrākṣamūrdhanirāvaraṇaguṇaprabhārāja Tathāgata.
At that time, in the presence of that Buddha,
I was a great vidyādhara, the king among rishis.
Having received this dhāraṇī from that Buddha,
at the moment it was obtained,
all the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared before one's eyes.
Upon seeing the Buddha appear,
one suddenly attains a wisdom never before experienced;
one should know that this mantra possesses such supernatural power.
It is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
If there are good men or good women who can diligently receive,
uphold, read, and recite it day and night so as not to forget it, [they shall attain great merit].
When reciting this dhāraṇī,
do not let the mind dwell upon other objects.
On every fifteenth day of the waxing moon or the eighth day of the waning moon, [perform the recitation].
Having bathed one's body and donned fresh, clean garments,
one should receive and maintain this dhāraṇī and perform the mudrā to protect the body.
Take pure mud to construct a square mandala measuring four cubits on each side; once the boundary has been established,
invite me, the One-Tufted Vidyārāja, to sit at the center of the mandala.
Burn incense, scatter flowers, and perform various offerings;
prostrate, repent, and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
One who maintains this vidyā shall immediately obtain ten kinds of karmic rewards in their present body.
What are the ten?
First, one’s body is always free from illness.
Second, one is constantly remembered by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Third, all wealth, clothing, food, and drink shall be spontaneously sufficient, never lacking in anything.
Fourth, one will be able to defeat enemies and adversaries.
Fifth, one will be able to cause all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Sixth, no malevolent poisons or any fevers shall be able to harm them.
Seventh, no weapons or staves shall be able to cause them injury.
Eighth, no water-related calamities shall be able to drown or sweep them away.
Ninth, fire cannot burn them.
Tenth, they do not undergo any untimely death.
These are called the ten.
Furthermore, one obtains four kinds of karmic rewards. What are these four?
First, one will not be harmed by birds or beasts.
Second, they shall not fall into hell.
Third, at the time of their death, they shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Fourth, after their lives end, they shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life.
"Bhagavān, I recall that more than incalculable kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Mandāravagandha Tathāgata.
At the time of that Buddha, I was a lay follower (upāsaka), a brāhmaṇa named Ekañjika."
In the presence of that Buddha, he further attained this Dharma;
he constantly preached the Dharma for hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Brahmās,
and there were none who did not submit and take refuge.
This is the Dharma-gate of the treasury of wisdom of all Buddhas’ great kindness, great compassion, great joy,
and great equanimity. By the power of this mantra,
one is able to rescue all sentient beings from imprisonment, confinement, shackles, fetters, and chains.
When facing execution, water, fire, or other such calamities,
and amidst all manner of suffering and affliction, I shall constantly protect and deliver you,
enabling you to attain liberation from all yakṣas, rākṣasīs, and the like.
By the power of this Dharma-seal dhāraṇī,
may all yakṣas, rākṣasīs, and others give rise to wholesome minds and become fully endowed with merit.
One is immediately able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such is its power that even if there were someone who has committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or other such sins, [they would likewise be transformed].
For one who recites and maintains this dhāraṇī even once,
all root transgressions and grave offenses without exception shall be completely extinguished;
how much more so for one who, in accordance with the Dharma, forms the mudrās and maintains it.
It should be known that such persons have heard this Dharma in the presence of ten million billion nayutas of Buddhas in the past,
and now hear it once again.
If there are good sons or good daughters, [who...]
For one who is able to receive, uphold, and remember [this] day and night without forgetting,
whatever aspirations the person seeks in their heart will be fulfilled without exception.
Whenever they desire to seek the supreme siddhi, it shall be attained.
On the eighth or fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
bathe with fragrant water and don fresh, clean garments;
bathe each time after using the toilet.
One must not defecate while wearing such pure garments.
When performing this rite, one shall not eat for that day.
One should perform the mudrā for binding the boundary and protecting the body.
Having performed the mudrā and recited the dhāraṇī until dawn,
one should place an image of the principal deity within the maṇḍala,
form the mudrā of invitation, and recite the mantra.
Hanging various multicolored banners and canopies,
and making offerings of incense and flowers,
one first enters the center of the maṇḍala.
One must reverently and with utmost sincerity invite the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Having sincerely repented, praised the Triple Gem, and prostrated,
one should spread a seat-covering before the image.
Kneeling with palms joined in reverence, one should make a sincere vow and form the *akṣamālā-mudrā*. Having formed it,
one should recite the mantra with single-minded concentration one thousand and eight times.
Next, holding an incense burner and burning incense, he said:
"In this place, there are no various offerings of superior flavors or food and drink;
I apologize for this with a sense of shame."
"World-Honored One, by the power of these dharma-seals and mantras,
whose names and titles are noble and difficult even to hear,
if there should be a person who recites the names of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas..."
Furthermore, there may be another who for a brief moment recites my name;
the merit of those two persons is exactly equal and no different.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One, if good sons and good daughters recite and maintain this vidyārāja-īkāryaṭa mantra day and night,
they shall be freed from all suffering and affliction, all obstacles and difficulties, and all fears.
Even the karmic obstacles of the three poisons will all be healed and eliminated;
how much more so for those who practice according to the Dharma.
One should know that such a person shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as if it were held within the palm of their hand.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
You are now able, toward all sentient beings..."
Arousing a mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion,
he desires to reveal this great dhāraṇī, the *Iccha-jata* Dharma-seal.
If a son of good family, by means of the power of the skillful methods of this dharma, [attains realization...]
They are fully able to rescue and liberate all sentient beings from all sickness, suffering, obstacles, difficulties, and fears of body,
speech, and mind, even establishing all sentient beings in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is certain and beyond doubt.
Son of good family, I too rejoice in these dharma-gates, such as this dhāraṇī-seal and others.
I have received these dharmas of yours, such as the mantras and mudrās;
I now likewise authorize them.
Son of good family, you may now expound them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
having received the Buddha’s approval, rose from his seat,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
He entered the *Anabhibhūta-samādhi*,
from the crown of his head emanated the Rākṣasa King Ekajaṭa,
who has three eyes and four arms.
All the eight classes of spirits and deities,
including the Great Powerful King of the Burning Summit (Dahumingwang), were struck with terror and fled in all directions;
each lost their original majesty and was no longer known where they were.
"May you grant us protection! May you grant us protection!
They all abandoned their malicious and harmful intentions.
From this day forward, together with their retinues, they took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
At that time, the king of ghosts, Jvalanāntamūrdhan, together with his retinue, having been subdued,
came to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara was;
joining his palms in reverent salutation, he addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
I possess a most profound and secret dhāraṇī mantra,
which is capable of crushing and destroying the celestial Māras,
as well as evil yakṣas, rākṣasīs, and malevolent spirits and ghosts.
It can also pacify various pestilences, water disasters, fire disasters, and bandits,
as well as quell all enemies and adversaries.
I pray that you will grant me permission to speak this dhāraṇī.
Then the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Ekajaṭī!
You have skillfully subdued the king of ghosts, Jvalamūrdhan, as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasīs, and others."
"You possess this secret root dhāraṇī;
listen to what you shall say, for now is the very time.
Then, Ekañjaṭa, having received the permission of the Great Sage, spoke.
Filled with great joy,
he circumambulated Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva three times and withdrew to sit to one side.
Before the presence of immeasurable great bodhisattvas, immeasurable Vajrapāṇis,
and the entire host of yakṣas and rākṣasas from the eight classes of spirits,
he then spoke this mantra:
Namaḥ samantabhadraya, namo 'ryāvalokiteśvarāya,
mañjudhāraye, mahāsattvāya, mahākāruṇikāya.
Namo 'kṣaya-mahā-rokṣi a-hṛdaya-māra-rokṣi mā-mukha-sarvakāryāṇi karohi me | Tadyathā | Oṃ ānandire ||
Oṃ jaye jaye yaśasvati mahāvijaye svāhā | mahārohiṇi svāhā | sarvavighnavināyakānāṃ ca svāhā ||
Dvihakṣarāya ṣṭa svāhā rakṣa rakṣa svāhā bhasmahaṭṭāya svāhā.
The heart-mantra is as follows:
Oṃ luḍra-yamuneriṇaye jaṭa jaṭaye hūṃ hūṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā. This is the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
*Īhe he īkajjaṭa mama mukhañjaye svāhā.* When Īkajjaṭa spoke this dhāraṇī, [the earth shook in six ways].
All the celestial palaces and the palaces of Māra,
as well as those of the nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasīs, and all other malevolent, poisonous, and harmful spirits and deities,
each led their own immeasurable retinues.
They all went before him and simultaneously raised their voices,
each saying, "We beg for our lives!
From this day forward, we and our retinues..."
Having forever severed evil thoughts,
those who vow to follow this matter and protect and uphold this dhāraṇī day and night shall not allow various ghosts and spirits to find any opportunity for harm.
"May you grant us fearlessness;
may we regain our original minds. Then, Ekajaṭī—
One should then form the mudrā of Bestowing Fearlessness for all the spirits and deities;
each shall then attain their original mind and pay homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
Next, they prostrated to the Nirmāṇakāya Ekajaṭī and each returned to their own palace.
At that time, Aikajaṭa addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
I possess a rite for the accomplishment of the seven-day offering altar.
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or virtuous sons who request this secret treasury of the Dharma, [I shall grant it].
One must certainly achieve great efficacy.
If kings develop a resolute mind and repent for their manifold transgressions, [they shall attain success].
One who wishes to behold the Dharma of the Great Place of Enlightenment (Mahāmaṇḍala) should first seek out a pure, spacious courtyard or a fine temple, monastery,
or shrine hall; even an open space will suffice once such a location has been found.
On the first day of the waxing moon, at the time of dawn,
the ācārya and his disciples shall bathe with fragrant water and,
taking various incenses and flowers, proceed to that location.
The Ācārya, holding a vajra in his hand,
asks the disciples in succession:
"Do you all resolutely desire to study the secret Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas?"
"Do not give rise to doubt.
The assembly replied, "We wish to study the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas;
we are resolute and sincere in our faith, and shall not harbor any doubts."
In this manner, there were three questions and three answers in succession.
Once the answering was completed,
the preceptor next performed the hand-seal (mudrā) over the incense burner, the water, and so forth.
Having recited the mantra,
holding an incense burner in hand and kneeling on the right knee,
one offers incense and addresses all the Buddhas, Prajñāpāramitā, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and devas.
"Along with all the lords of the earth and the paths of karma,
this ground is now my domain.
I now wish to establish a seven-day and seven-night assembly for the ritual altar of the Great Way."
I make offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm,
as well as to the great assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Prajñāpāramitā,
the Vajra Deities, and others.
Leading all the assemblies,
he took up the various proofs for the sake of definitively establishing the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the treasury of all secret teachings.
I wish to perform the rite for establishing the boundary to protect this body.
Within this enclosure— in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—
all those vināyakas, evil spirits, and malevolent ghosts who destroy the True Dharma.
All must depart to a place seven *li* outside the boundary.
As for the protective deities, spirits,
and ghosts who uphold the True Dharma and who bring benefit to my Buddha-dharma:
He dwelt as he pleased.
Having spoken these words,
he proceeded according to the ritual of that Mañjuśrī-muṇḍa.
Having performed the ritual of expelling obstructors and established the boundary,
one should immediately have all impure soil, bones, hair, charcoal, husks, shards, rubble, and other such things excavated from within an area of ten cubits.
If it is superior ground, one should dig to a depth of one *vitasti*; if middling ground, one cubit (*hasta*);
if inferior ground, two cubits;
and if very inferior ground, one should dig to a depth of three cubits.
Once all impure things have been completely removed,
take fine, pure earth mixed with various powdered incenses;
pack it firmly to make the foundation level, and ensure the base is as high as possible.
On the second and third days,
smear the ground with clay.
On the fourth day, use cow dung mixed with fragrant mud.
Having finished coating the ground,
next take the divine cord and wrap it once around the four sides at eight cubits;
mark a dot at each of the four corners.
Furthermore, using a divine cord,
[draw lines] from the northeast corner to the southwest corner,
and from the southeast corner to the northwest corner.
Cross and tie them together.
At the intersection of the lines,
mark a point below and dig the earth to a depth of about one span (*vitasti*).
One should bury therein the five treasures as well as the five grains.
As for the five treasures:
first, gold; second, silver; third, pearls; fourth, coral; and fifth, amber.
Regarding the five grains: first, large barley; second, small wheat; third, rice; fourth, small beans; and fifth, sesame.
Wrap these grains together with a single piece of silk, tie the silk with thread of five colors, and bury it.
One end of each of these five-colored threads emerges from the ground to a length of about five finger-widths;
these precious objects have never before emerged.
Next, perform the great boundary-binding (*mahā-sīmābandha*).
Regarding the ritual for binding the boundary:
holding the *vajra*, walk three times swiftly around the exterior of the altar in a clockwise direction.
Expel the vināyakas and perform various boundary-markings;
seal the ground with mudrās.
In the east, west, south, north, above, and below,
recite the mantra and perform the mudrās;
the rites for announcing, expelling obstructors, and establishing the boundary (sīmābandha) are as explained on the first day.
Following the ritual procedures for Mañjuśrī,
the method for establishing the boundary on the fifth day is the same as that of the fourth day;
furthermore, one should smear the ground with cow dung.
As for the method of smearing the ground, one should rub it with the right hand turning clockwise;
do not rub it with the left hand turning counter-clockwise.
All other ritual procedures are the same as those of the fourth day.
Next, on the sixth day, the ācārya bathes.
First, he enters the maṇḍala and selects two disciples who are exceptionally intelligent;
they also bathe thoroughly, put on new clean garments, and enter the maṇḍala following him.
Having finished mixing white powder with sandalwood water,
dye the divine cord (śūtra) within that liquid. Then,
have a disciple hold the end of the cord at the northeast corner of the altar.
Precisely at the point where the corner was first marked,
the Ācārya next takes one end of the cord and places it on the southeast corner of the altar.
Precisely at the point where the corner was first lowered,
he quickly pulled it taut to the ground and had a disciple pinch the center of the cord.
They are spread upon the ground.
Next, the disciple from the northeast corner rises and sits facing the southwest corner.
Proceed as before.
Next, the ācārya rises from the southeast corner and sits facing the northwest corner.
Furthermore, as before, the disciple next arises at the southwest corner,
sits facing east, and likewise follows the previous ritual method; then,
he first marks the location for the grid lines.
Moving from the outside toward the inside,
leave a space of one cubit (*hasta*) and again encircle and mark it according to the previous method.
Next, take a divine cord (*sūtra*) eight cubits long.
Bend the middle [finger] toward one side of the altar;
place a single dot at each joint,
and further bend the two elbows of the cord.
From the center point on one side of the mandala,
measure to the left and right to mark two further points;
next, do the same for the gate on that side.
The cord for the altar opening is five finger-widths [in width].
Next, bend the door-opening further toward the left and right by five finger-widths.
Next, on both sides of the door,
a space approximately five finger-widths wide should be made.
Then, along the outer edge of the door.
Draw it straight.
If one side is thus, the other three sides should be understood accordingly.
Next, construct the central court.
The outer cord is four cubits [long].
Within that outer enclosure,
the inner cord is aligned with the middle cord.
Between the two ropes, leave a path of one cubit wide.
The doors of the inner courtyard are opened on all four sides;
they extend toward the left and right for a total of three finger-widths.
The method for joining the divine lines outside the gate is also according to the previous method.
Within that middle courtyard, it is square.
At a distance of one cubit from the outer boundary,
further mark the spirit-line and delineate the mandala.
At the exact center, construct a courtyard measuring two cubits;
do not provide a door.
Next, the ācārya [uses] five-colored thread.
Recite the mantra once and tie one of the fifty-five knots;
use the Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara Dhāraṇī.
The mantra is as follows:

*Īrye bhagavann ārya-vajracarcikā-svaramudrāmudrita-sattvamanusmara siddhamanusmara tadyathā | Naju naju kini kini hini hini nuru nuru miru miru juru juru duru duru suru suru muru muru vara vara modaya modaya hiri miri nicini sidhyantu me mantraṃ svāhā.* Next, using silk cloth.
Wrap [the objects] in the five precious gems along with seeds of the five grains,
and tie them with a mantra-cord using threads of five colors;
wrap each one individually according to the number of people, whether many or few.
Next, erect one pole at each of the four corners of the maṇḍala and two poles at the western gate; then,
wrap and tie a cord around the poles at the four corners.
Upon those lines, hang multicolored banners. Above the altar,
tie banners to the four cardinal directions— east, west, south, and north— and to the four intermediate directions,
adorning them with an interlacing network.
Outside the enclosure of the altar, to the south of the western gate,
dig a fire pit two chi away [from the wall],
measuring two chi in length, width, and depth.
Within that furnace,
leave behind a mound of earth;
upon this mound, fashion a lotus seat out of scented clay.
On the following day at sunset,
the ācārya had all the disciples bathe; thereafter,
the ācārya performed the great ritual boundary-binding (mahā-sīmābandha).
On the following day at the appointed hour, one shall invoke all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajras.
Place a single image of the Buddha at the center of the maṇḍala;
place Avalokiteśvara in the north and Vajrapāṇi in the south.
One should make offerings with various kinds of incense, flowers, five trays of food and drink, and sixteen oil lamps. Next,
one should spread a fresh, clean mat outside the western gate.
Next, the ācārya calls the disciples and forms the protection-of-the-body mudrā,
reciting the mantra seven times for each one.
Having individually placed the mudrās upon the heads, both shoulders, heart, throat, space between the eyebrows, hairline, and the back of the head of each disciple,
and having thus completed the protection of their bodies,
he had the disciples take their seats upon the mats.
Facing east, sit down.
Next, take incense, flowers, and white mustard seeds.
The ācārya holds the white mustard seeds and recites the mantra seven times.
He struck each of the disciples on the head in succession.
Having completed the striking three times,
he further bestowed the protection of the body by means of the seal of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva.
The mantra is:
Oṃ hāya-gri-vāsamat-āmṛte hūṃ. Next, the ācārya kneels and asks the eldest disciple:
He then asked, "Do you now wish to study this Dharma?
The disciple replied, "I do."
In this manner, the questions were asked of the disciples in succession according to the ritual procedure as before.
Next, the ācārya held up scented water and poured it over the head of each disciple one by one, covering them.
He places his right hand upon the chest of each disciple one by one,
reciting the mantra of Avalokiteśvara Hayagrīva.
Next, he takes up the mantra-cord.
Tie them each to the arms of their respective disciples—
on the left for men and on the right for women.
Next is the incense of *sāba* tree sap.
He then consecrates the bodies of the disciples in succession.
Having completed the sprinkling of the scented water by circling it three times to the right,
he next circles a flaming torch, also according to the previous method.
Next, he gives each a tooth-stick eight finger-widths long.
After the flowers have been bestowed,
he has the disciples sit in a row facing east.
Instruct the disciples to cast flowers forward.
Next, they should chew a tooth-stick and likewise cast it forward as before.
If the tip of the flower points toward the person, it is auspicious.
If the tooth-stick points toward the east when discarded, one should know that demonic obstacles will arise;
if it points toward the south or north, it is unfavorable.
It is auspicious if the part chewed faces the practitioner.
If one faces east, it is known that demonic obstacles are departing.
The rest is according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* ritual.
Next, provide them with water for washing their hands.
Each is made to drink the water of the vajra vow;
they respectfully decline, yet eventually drink it.
Next, the ācārya enters within the maṇḍala.
The Bodhisattvas, Vajradharas, and others addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The disciples wish to enter the maṇḍala again tomorrow to perform extensive offerings."
"May all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajra-devas, and others, please ascend to their original palaces.

Hereafter, when offerings are presented, may you all descend to accept these manifold offerings. Thus it is said three times. Thereupon, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, and various devas within the maṇḍala are dismissed.
Next, the ācārya proceeds to the edge of the maṇḍala and sits facing south.
He places a single fire-pit before him and recites the Hayagrīva mantra.
Burn white mustard seeds—one for each mantra—repeating this one hundred and eight times.
At that time, all the disciples' transgressions will be extinguished.
Next, the ācārya [bestows them] upon two disciples.
During one night, he spread five-colored powders within the mandala according to the five directions;
the seats for all other worthy deities were arranged according to the methods of the three families.
Next, perform the protection of the body using the Hayagrīva mudrā.
Recite: Oṃ haya graṭa hūṃ.
Then hold the vajra and perform the Amṛtakuṇḍalī body mudrā three times.
Circumambulate clockwise along the outer edge of the mandala.
Next, perform the boundary-binding of the ground (bhūmibandha) in sequence for the four directions, above, and below.
